newsitem.title: CANADA: Bankruptcies send chill through Canada gas market.
newsitem.headline: Bankruptcies send chill through Canada gas market.

text.p: A spate of recent bankruptcies among small Canadian natural gas marketers has sent a chill through the Alberta spot market and underscored the dangers of speculation when prices turn volatile.
A flash flood of red ink hit the Canadian gas market in November when spot prices doubled amid high gas demand in export markets and frigid weather in Alberta.

The spike in prices meant unexpectedly high returns for any company with its own gas to sell. But it also caused a major cash crunch for small trading firms without strong financial backing. Companies with short positions taken as recently as last summer were particularly vulnerable.
"Anyone on the long side made windfall profits and anyone on the short side is out of business," said a trader with the Canadian subsidiary of a large U.S. marketing firm.
As prices remained volatile, more financial failures were likely, marketing sources said.
"It's the talk of the town. I can't see why there wouldn't be more (failures)," said the president of another small Canadian energy marketer. "But there are not that many small players left"

Over the past month, private marketer Multi-Energies Inc went bankrupt, newly formed NESI Energy Marketing Canada Ltd filed for protection from creditors and Tarpon Gas Marketing Ltd was placed into receivership.

Also, Kentucky-based LG&E Natural Inc, a unit of LG&E Energy Corp, launched a C$210 million lawsuit against the former vice-president of its Canadian subsidary, alleging he made unauthorized trades resulting in losses of US$17 million. The executive has argued he had authorization to make the trades.
Industry experts said the financial bloodbath spotlighted a big reason why North America's natural gas marketing companies had been merging in the past year to form mega-marketers.

Big companies with strong balance sheets and creditworthiness could withstand big price spikes and crashes, while smaller players could find themselves exposed past their limits in a matter of days, said the trader.
He noted that the price of Alberta gas for delivery in the winter months had recently moved by as much as C$0.10 a gigajoule with each trade, even in deals for small amounts of gas.
Gas prices in the province, which suffered a two-year depression until this autumn, had usually moved by just pennies, even when volumes were high.

"They got caught," said natural gas analyst Brent Friedenburg, president of Calgary-based Friedenburg and Associates. "They were trading gas and making commitments on one side -- either the sell or the buy side -- and not covering themselves on the other side," Friedenburg said.
The unexpected jump in prices also caught short-sellers by surprise, forcing them to buy gas supply in the spot market at prices far higher than projected when deals were made.

In a short sale, traders borrow gas or any other commodity or security, to sell into the market, speculating that its price will drop over time. If it does, the trader can buy it back at a lower price and pocket the difference.
The trader said many short deals for term gas last summer were done in the C$1.30 to C$1.40 per gigajoule range. But spot prices spiked in November to well over C$2.
"Now there aren't as many players willing to trade with anyone with less than perfect credit," he said.
